context: An e-commerce platform runs a distributed product catalog cache across 3 data centers (US-East, US-West, EU-West). The cache serves product prices, inventory counts, and availability status. Current setup: eventual consistency with a 30-second replication lag between data centers. Problem: during flash sales, inventory counts can be stale by 30 seconds, leading to overselling (customers purchase items that are already sold out, requiring refunds). Last flash sale: 3% of orders were oversold, costing $45,000 in refunds and customer service. Two proposals: (A) Switch to strong consistency (synchronous replication) — eliminates overselling but adds 80-120ms latency per read (cross-region round trip) and means a data center outage makes the cache unavailable. (B) Keep eventual consistency but add a 'reservation' system — when inventory drops below a threshold, route purchases through a single authoritative node for that product, adding latency only for low-stock items.
question: Should the team switch to strong consistency or implement the reservation system?
expert_answer: Implement the reservation system (option B). It addresses the actual problem (overselling during low inventory) without imposing a latency penalty on the 97% of reads that are not inventory-sensitive.
expert_reasoning: Strong consistency (A) is a global solution to a local problem. Overselling only occurs when inventory is low — the vast majority of product reads (prices, descriptions, availability for in-stock items) do not need strong consistency and should not pay the 80-120ms latency tax. The reservation system targets the precise failure mode: when inventory for a specific product drops below a threshold (e.g., 10 units), subsequent purchases for THAT product are routed to the authoritative node, adding latency only for the small percentage of requests that could oversell. This preserves the performance benefits of eventual consistency for 97%+ of traffic while eliminating overselling for the critical low-inventory window. The availability argument also favors option B: strong consistency means a US-East outage makes the entire cache unavailable (all reads fail until failover), while eventual consistency with reservations degrades gracefully (reads continue from other DCs, only low-stock purchases are affected during failover). For an e-commerce platform, 'slow checkout for one item' is far better than 'entire catalog unavailable.'
anti_pattern: Switching to strong consistency because 'we cannot tolerate any data staleness.' This treats the 30-second replication lag as the root cause, when the actual root cause is purchasing against stale inventory counts. Strong consistency adds 80-120ms to EVERY read — including product browsing, search results, and cart displays that have no consistency requirement. The 3% overselling rate becomes a 100% latency penalty. Worse, strong consistency couples availability to the slowest replica: network partitions between data centers cause complete cache unavailability rather than graceful degradation.
